I read the draft as a shopper on the product page and checked each sentence.

- **"Peppermint. Just peppermint leaves, nothing else."** This is an ingredient fact, which the product team checks and the policy allows as written.
- **"Cool and clean after a big meal."** This describes how the tea tastes and feels. It doesn't say the tea aids digestion, settles the stomach or has any effect on the body, so it isn't a health claim. It would become one if reworded to something like "helps digestion" or "soothes your stomach", so keep it as it is.
- **"Certified organic by the Soil Association."** This matches the approved claim word for word. The certificate is on file and was renewed in 2026.

I found no superlatives, guarantees, numbers, testimonials, urgency or environmental claims. None of the banned words appear, and the tone is plain and unhurried. It's UK-appropriate and not repetitive, and nothing needs a label on a brand-owned product page.

The copy is fine to publish. Per the policy, Sam still approves everything public.
